passages.title: The living speaker answers fear and makes the assemblies responsible for hearing
passages.summary: The book calls itself a revelation of Jesus Christ, sent to John. John writes to seven assemblies in Asia. He was on the island of Patmos because of God’s word. On the Lord’s day he hears a voice like a trumpet. He sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands. His eyes are like fire, and a sharp sword comes from his mouth. John falls at his feet like a dead man. The figure tells him to write, and says the lampstands are the seven assemblies.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Revelation names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church lesson reads these images as testimony that Christ lives and guides the Church. Why does the living speaker answer fear before giving the command to write?

contextNote.title: The living speaker answers fear and makes the assemblies responsible for hearing
contextNote.text: Verse 17 shows John’s response to the vision: he falls as though dead. The speaker lays his right hand on him and says not to fear. Verses 17–18 give the reason in what the speaker says of himself. He is the first and the last, and the Living one. He was dead and is alive forever. He holds the keys of Death and Hades. Only then does verse 19 give the order to write.

passages.title: Different messages test endurance and conduct without making earlier faithfulness sufficient
passages.summary: John writes four messages from Christ. Ephesus has worked hard and tested false apostles but has left its first love. Smyrna is poor and yet rich, and will suffer for ten days. Pergamum holds fast where Satan’s throne is, yet some hold the teaching of Balaam. Thyatira has love and service but tolerates a woman called Jezebel. Each message ends with a promise to the one who overcomes. Each tells those with ears to hear what the Spirit says.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects these distinct messages with Christ's knowledge of personal trials. Why does praise for endurance fail to remove the need for repentance?

contextNote.title: Different messages test endurance and conduct without making earlier faithfulness sufficient
contextNote.text: Verses 2–3 praise Ephesus for work, endurance, and testing false apostles. Verse 4 still holds one thing against it: it left its first love. Verse 5 gives three commands in order. Remember where you fell from, repent, and do the first works. Past labor does not replace them. The warning is concrete: the lampstand will be moved from its place. In 1:20 a lampstand is an assembly, so the assembly itself is at risk.

passages.title: Reputation and wealth can conceal failure while small power can coexist with faithfulness
passages.summary: John writes three more messages. Sardis has a name for being alive and is dead. A few there have not soiled their clothes. Philadelphia has little power, has kept Christ’s word, and has an open door. Laodicea is neither cold nor hot and will be spat out. It says it is rich, yet it is poor, blind, and naked. Christ counsels it to buy gold, white clothes, and eye salve from him. He stands at the door and knocks.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects these promises with Christ's help in overcoming trials. How can a reputation for life or wealth conceal the condition the speaker names?

contextNote.title: Reputation and wealth can conceal failure while small power can coexist with faithfulness
contextNote.text: Verses 15–17 give Laodicea no praise. It is lukewarm, and it does not know its own poverty. Verse 19 explains the tone. The speaker reproves and disciplines those he loves. So the rebuke is evidence of love and not of rejection. The command that follows is short: be zealous and repent. Verse 20 shows him still at the door, knocking and offering a shared meal.

passages.title: Heavenly worship places created power beneath the one who gives all things existence
passages.summary: John sees a door open in heaven and is called up. One sits on a throne there and shines like jasper and sardius. A rainbow surrounds the throne. Twenty-four elders sit on thrones in white with golden crowns. Seven lamps burn, and a sea like glass lies before the throne. Four living creatures, like a lion, a calf, a man, and an eagle, never rest. They say, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty.” The elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.

lds.text: Doctrine and Covenants 77:1 reads the sea of glass as the sanctified earth. Why do the elders surrender crowns while praising the source of created life?

contextNote.title: Heavenly worship places created power beneath the one who gives all things existence
contextNote.text: Verse 10 shows the elders laying their crowns before the throne. Verse 11 gives their words, and the words explain the act. God is worthy to receive glory, honor, and power. The reason given is creation. He created all things, and they exist because he willed it. A crown is a sign of rule. The elders give theirs up to the one who made all things.

passages.title: The slain Lamb's worthiness changes grief into shared praise and hope of redeemed life
passages.summary: John sees a book in the right hand of the one on the throne. It is sealed with seven seals. An angel asks who is worthy to open it, and no one is found. John weeps. An elder says the Lion of the tribe of Judah has overcome. John looks and sees a Lamb standing as though it had been slain. The Lamb takes the book, and the creatures and elders sing a new song. Countless angels and every creature join the praise.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson reads the sealed book through Christ's unique role in salvation. How does the Lamb's death explain worthiness to open the book?

contextNote.title: The slain Lamb's worthiness changes grief into shared praise and hope of redeemed life
contextNote.text: Verse 4 shows John weeping because no one can open the book. Verse 5 announces a Lion, and verse 6 shows a slain Lamb. The song in verse 9 says why this Lamb is worthy. The reason is not strength: “for you were killed.” His blood bought people for God. They come from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Verse 10 adds what they become: a kingdom and priests.

passages.title: Opened seals expose death and suffering while the killed witnesses ask for judgment
passages.summary: The Lamb opens six seals. A rider on a white horse goes out to conquer. A red horse takes peace from the earth, and a black horse brings scarce food. A pale horse carries Death, and Hades follows. At the fifth seal John sees under the altar those killed for God’s word. They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. At the sixth seal the earth quakes and the sky rolls up. Kings and slaves hide and ask who is able to stand.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson connects opened seals with the Savior's authority. Why do the killed witnesses still ask how long judgment will wait?

contextNote.title: Opened seals expose death and suffering while the killed witnesses ask for judgment
contextNote.text: The first four seals release conquest, war, scarcity, and death (verses 1–8). The fifth shows the victims: those killed for God’s word and their testimony (verse 9). Verse 10 gives them a voice. They call God holy and true, and they ask “How long.” They ask him to judge; they do not avenge themselves. Verse 11 gives a robe and an answer, and the answer is to wait. More of their fellow servants are yet to be killed.

passages.title: Sealing and shelter answer the question of standing through belonging and rescue
passages.summary: Four angels hold back the winds until God’s servants are sealed. John hears the number: 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. Then he sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation. They wear white robes and hold palm branches. They cry that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. An elder says they have come out of the great suffering. They washed their robes white in the Lamb’s blood. They will never hunger or thirst again.

He leads them to springs of life-giving waters. The last line names God’s own act: he wipes every tear from their eyes.

passages.title: Prayer enters the throne scene before trumpet judgments damage the world's ordinary supports
passages.summary: The Lamb opens the seventh seal, and heaven is silent for half an hour. Seven angels receive seven trumpets. Another angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints at the golden altar. He fills the censer with fire and throws it to the earth. The first trumpet burns a third of the earth and trees. The second and third strike a third of the sea and the rivers. The fourth darkens a third of the sun, moon, and stars. An eagle cries woe for the three trumpets still to come.

contextNote.title: Prayer enters the throne scene before trumpet judgments damage the world's ordinary supports
contextNote.text: In 6:10 the killed witnesses asked how long. Chapter 8 opens with silence, and then with prayer (verses 1 and 3). Verse 3 puts the saints’ prayers on the golden altar with incense. Verse 4 says the smoke and the prayers rise before God. Verse 5 follows directly. The angel fills that censer with altar fire and throws it down. Only after that do the trumpets sound (verse 6), so the prayers come first.

passages.title: Restricted torment and deadly plagues reveal that suffering does not automatically produce repentance
passages.summary: At the fifth trumpet a star falls and opens the pit of the abyss. Smoke rises, and locusts come out with power like scorpions. They may not kill, but they torment people without God’s seal for five months. Their king is called Abaddon, or Apollyon. At the sixth trumpet four angels bound at the Euphrates are released. An army of horsemen kills a third of mankind with fire and sulfur. The survivors do not repent of idols. They do not repent of murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson asks how lasting divine rule gives hope amid plagues. Why does destruction fail to produce repentance in the surviving people?

contextNote.title: Restricted torment and deadly plagues reveal that suffering does not automatically produce repentance
contextNote.text: The two trumpets bring torment and then death (verses 5 and 18). Verse 20 reports what the survivors do, and it is nothing new. They do not repent of the works of their hands. The verse describes the idols by material: gold, silver, brass, stone, and wood. They cannot see, hear, or walk. Verse 21 adds the wrongs against people that go with them.

passages.title: The eaten book makes renewed prophecy both received sweetness and bodily bitterness
passages.summary: A mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow on his head. He holds a little open book and stands on sea and land. Seven thunders speak, and John is told not to write their words. The angel swears that there will be no more delay. A voice tells John to take the book from the angel. The angel says it will taste sweet and turn the stomach bitter. John eats it, and it is so. He is told he must prophesy again about many peoples and kings.

contextNote.title: The eaten book makes renewed prophecy both received sweetness and bodily bitterness
contextNote.text: Verse 9 tells John to eat the book before he speaks. Verse 10 reports two effects in order. In the mouth it is sweet as honey. In the stomach it turns bitter. Ezekiel also ate a sweet scroll that held laments (Ezekiel 2:10; 3:3). Verse 11 connects the eating with the task: John must prophesy again. The message is taken in first, and it costs the one who carries it.

passages.title: Killed witnesses return to life before the final trumpet announces lasting rule
passages.summary: John is given a reed to measure God’s temple. Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth for 1,260 days. Fire comes from their mouths, and they can shut the sky. The beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie in the street. People celebrate for three and a half days. Then the breath of life enters them, and they go up to heaven. An earthquake follows. The seventh trumpet sounds, and voices say the world’s kingdom has become the Lord’s.

contextNote.text: The chapter first shows witnesses killed and mocked (verses 7–10). Verse 11 reverses it: the breath of life from God enters them. Verse 15 then sounds the last of the seven trumpets. It brings no new plague in this verse. It brings an announcement from great voices in heaven. The world’s kingdom has become the kingdom of the Lord and his Christ. In verse 17 the elders say God has taken his power and reigned.

The woman flees to the wilderness. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him down to the earth. A voice calls him the accuser and says the brothers overcame him. The dragon pursues the woman, and the earth helps her. He goes to make war on the rest of her offspring.

contextNote.text: Verses 7–9 show the dragon thrown out of heaven by Michael. Verse 10 calls him the accuser of the brothers. Verse 11 says how the brothers themselves overcame him. Two means are named: the Lamb’s blood and the word of their testimony. They did not love their life, even to death. So their victory does not mean they were spared. Verse 12 confirms it: the dragon comes down in great wrath.

passages.title: Worship becomes coercion when deceptive signs and economic exclusion support the beast's power
passages.summary: A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads. The dragon gives it power, and one head has a healed death wound. The whole earth marvels and worships it. It speaks blasphemies and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb. It works signs and makes people worship the first beast’s image. It puts a mark on the right hand or forehead of all. The number of the beast is 666.

contextNote.text: Verses 13–15 show the second beast using signs and the threat of death. Verses 16–17 add a quieter pressure. Everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, receives a mark. Verse 17 states its use: no one can buy or sell without it. Worship is thus enforced through the market. Verse 10 has already told the saints what this requires: endurance and faith. Verse 18 calls for wisdom about the number.

passages.summary: John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name. They sing a new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. An angel flies with eternal good news for every nation. A second says Babylon has fallen. A third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath. A voice blesses the dead who die in the Lord. One like a son of man reaps the earth’s harvest. An angel gathers the grapes and throws them into the winepress of God’s wrath.

Two kinds of book are opened. The books record works, and the dead are judged by them. The other is the book of life. Verse 13 adds that the sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead.

The one on the throne says he is making all things new. An angel shows John the city, with twelve gates named for Israel’s tribes. Its twelve foundations bear the names of the Lamb’s apostles. The city is pure gold, and its gates are pearls. It has no temple or sun, for God and the Lamb light it.

Then four things end: death, mourning, crying, and pain. The verse gives the reason: “The first things have passed away.” The book has shown those first things in its seals, trumpets, and bowls. Verse 5 answers them with one sentence from the throne: all things new.

passages.summary: The angel shows John the river of life flowing from the throne. The tree of life grows beside it, and its leaves heal the nations. God’s servants will see his face, and there will be no night. Jesus says he is coming soon. John falls before the angel and is again told to worship God. He is told not to seal the book, for the time is near. A warning forbids adding to or taking from the book’s words. The book ends with a prayer for the Lord Jesus to come.

contextNote.text: Verse 1 shows the river of the water of life, and verse 2 the tree. Verse 17 turns the vision into an invitation. The Spirit and the bride say “Come.” Each hearer is told to pass the word on. Then the thirsty are invited, and the water is free. In 21:6 the one on the throne made the same offer. Chapter 18 showed a city where everything had a price.

events.title: The living speaker answers fear and makes the assemblies responsible for hearing
events.summary: The book calls itself a revelation of Jesus Christ, sent to John. John writes to seven assemblies in Asia. He was on the island of Patmos because of God’s word. On the Lord’s day he hears a voice like a trumpet. He sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands. His eyes are like fire, and a sharp sword comes from his mouth. John falls at his feet like a dead man. The figure tells him to write, and says the lampstands are the seven assemblies.
events.detail: Verse 17 shows John’s response to the vision: he falls as though dead. The speaker lays his right hand on him and says not to fear. Verses 17–18 give the reason in what the speaker says of himself. He is the first and the last, and the Living one. He was dead and is alive forever. He holds the keys of Death and Hades. Only then does verse 19 give the order to write.

events.title: Different messages test endurance and conduct without making earlier faithfulness sufficient
events.summary: John writes four messages from Christ. Ephesus has worked hard and tested false apostles but has left its first love. Smyrna is poor and yet rich, and will suffer for ten days. Pergamum holds fast where Satan’s throne is, yet some hold the teaching of Balaam. Thyatira has love and service but tolerates a woman called Jezebel. Each message ends with a promise to the one who overcomes. Each tells those with ears to hear what the Spirit says.
events.detail: Verses 2–3 praise Ephesus for work, endurance, and testing false apostles. Verse 4 still holds one thing against it: it left its first love. Verse 5 gives three commands in order. Remember where you fell from, repent, and do the first works. Past labor does not replace them. The warning is concrete: the lampstand will be moved from its place. In 1:20 a lampstand is an assembly, so the assembly itself is at risk.

events.summary: John writes three more messages. Sardis has a name for being alive and is dead. A few there have not soiled their clothes. Philadelphia has little power, has kept Christ’s word, and has an open door. Laodicea is neither cold nor hot and will be spat out. It says it is rich, yet it is poor, blind, and naked. Christ counsels it to buy gold, white clothes, and eye salve from him. He stands at the door and knocks.

So the rebuke is evidence of love and not of rejection. The command that follows is short: be zealous and repent. Verse 20 shows him still at the door, knocking and offering a shared meal.

Four living creatures, like a lion, a calf, a man, and an eagle, never rest. They say, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty.” The elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne.

events.detail: Verse 9 tells John to eat the book before he speaks. Verse 10 reports two effects in order. In the mouth it is sweet as honey. In the stomach it turns bitter. Ezekiel also ate a sweet scroll that held laments (Ezekiel 2:10; 3:3). Verse 11 connects the eating with the task: John must prophesy again. The message is taken in first, and it costs the one who carries it.

events.title: Killed witnesses return to life before the final trumpet announces lasting rule
events.summary: John is given a reed to measure God’s temple. Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth for 1,260 days. Fire comes from their mouths, and they can shut the sky. The beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie in the street. People celebrate for three and a half days. Then the breath of life enters them, and they go up to heaven. An earthquake follows. The seventh trumpet sounds, and voices say the world’s kingdom has become the Lord’s.
events.detail: The chapter first shows witnesses killed and mocked (verses 7–10). Verse 11 reverses it: the breath of life from God enters them. Verse 15 then sounds the last of the seven trumpets. It brings no new plague in this verse. It brings an announcement from great voices in heaven. The world’s kingdom has become the kingdom of the Lord and his Christ. In verse 17 the elders say God has taken his power and reigned.

events.title: The dragon's defeat leads into continued danger while testimony explains the saints' victory
events.summary: A woman clothed with the sun cries out in labor. A great red dragon with seven heads waits to devour her child. Her son, who will rule the nations, is caught up to God. The woman flees to the wilderness. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him down to the earth. A voice calls him the accuser and says the brothers overcame him. The dragon pursues the woman, and the earth helps her. He goes to make war on the rest of her offspring.
events.detail: Verses 7–9 show the dragon thrown out of heaven by Michael. Verse 10 calls him the accuser of the brothers. Verse 11 says how the brothers themselves overcame him. Two means are named: the Lamb’s blood and the word of their testimony. They did not love their life, even to death. So their victory does not mean they were spared. Verse 12 confirms it: the dragon comes down in great wrath.

events.title: Worship becomes coercion when deceptive signs and economic exclusion support the beast's power
events.summary: A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads. The dragon gives it power, and one head has a healed death wound. The whole earth marvels and worships it. It speaks blasphemies and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb. It works signs and makes people worship the first beast’s image. It puts a mark on the right hand or forehead of all. The number of the beast is 666.
events.detail: Verses 13–15 show the second beast using signs and the threat of death. Verses 16–17 add a quieter pressure. Everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, receives a mark. Verse 17 states its use: no one can buy or sell without it. Worship is thus enforced through the market. Verse 10 has already told the saints what this requires: endurance and faith. Verse 18 calls for wisdom about the number.

events.title: Following the Lamb contrasts with enforced worship while harvest images announce judgment
events.summary: John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name. They sing a new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. An angel flies with eternal good news for every nation. A second says Babylon has fallen. A third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath. A voice blesses the dead who die in the Lord. One like a son of man reaps the earth’s harvest. An angel gathers the grapes and throws them into the winepress of God’s wrath.
events.detail: Chapter 13 showed worship of the beast enforced by a mark. Verses 9–11 warn what that worship leads to. Verse 12 turns to the saints and names what the moment asks: perseverance. It describes them by two things they keep. They keep God’s commandments, and they keep the faith of Jesus. Verse 13 adds a blessing for those who die in the Lord. They rest from their labors, and their works follow them.

events.title: The victors' song praises just rule before the final plagues leave the heavenly temple
events.summary: John sees seven angels with the seven last plagues. Those who overcame the beast stand on a sea of glass mixed with fire. They hold harps of God. They sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb. The song says all nations will come and worship. The temple of the tabernacle of the testimony opens in heaven. One of the living creatures gives the angels seven golden bowls of wrath. Smoke fills the temple, and no one can enter until the plagues end.
events.detail: Verse 1 says the last plagues complete God’s wrath. Before they fall, verse 2 shows the victors standing by a sea. Verse 3 names their song after Moses and after the Lamb. Israel sang with Moses beside the sea after its rescue (Exodus 15:1). The words praise God’s works as great and his ways as righteous and true. Verse 4 adds that all nations will come and worship. So the judgments that follow are introduced as just.

events.title: Repeated refusal of repentance interrupts the bowls with a warning to remain alert
events.summary: A voice tells the seven angels to pour out the bowls. Sores, a sea of blood, and rivers of blood follow. The sun scorches people, and they blaspheme and do not repent. The beast’s kingdom is darkened. The Euphrates dries up for the kings from the east. Three unclean spirits like frogs gather the kings for war. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying, “It is done,” and a great earthquake. Great hail falls, and people blaspheme God.
events.detail: Verses 9 and 11 report twice that people did not repent. Verses 13–14 show spirits gathering kings for war. Verse 15 breaks into the account in the first person. The speaker says he comes like a thief. No time is given, so the instruction is to watch. The blessing is for one who stays awake and keeps his clothes. Verse 16 then returns to the gathering of the kings.

events.title: The city's powerful partners become agents of its ruin rather than a secure protection
events.summary: An angel shows John a woman seated on a scarlet beast. She wears purple and gold and is drunk with the saints’ blood. Her name is “Babylon the Great.” The angel explains the mystery. The beast’s seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings. The ten horns are ten kings who give their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and he will overcome them. The horns will hate the woman, the great city, and burn her.
events.detail: Verses 12–13 describe ten kings who give their power to the beast. Verse 14 states their aim and its outcome in one sentence. They make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb overcomes them. The reason is his rank: Lord of lords and King of kings. The verse also names those with him: called, chosen, and faithful. Verse 16 then shows the same kings turning on the woman. Verse 17 says God put this into their hearts.

events.title: The city's trade and violence explain why departure must mean refusing participation
events.summary: An angel cries that Babylon the great has fallen. Another voice calls God’s people to come out of her. Her sins have reached heaven, and she will be repaid double. Kings who shared her luxury weep at the smoke of her burning. Merchants weep because no one buys their cargo. The list runs from gold and spices to the bodies and souls of people. Shipmasters cry out that such wealth was ruined in one hour. A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, and the city’s music stops.
events.detail: Verse 3 says nations, kings, and merchants all shared in the city’s wealth. Verse 4 speaks to a different group: “my people.” They are told to come out of her. Two reasons are given. They must not share in her sins, and they must not receive her plagues. The cargo list shows what sharing would mean. It ends in verse 13 with people’s bodies and souls.

events.title: Wedding joy and the rider's judgment replace the city's splendor and deceptive rule
events.summary: A great crowd in heaven praises God for judging the great prostitute. A voice announces the Lamb’s marriage, and his wife has made herself ready. John falls to worship the angel and is told to worship God. Heaven opens, and a rider called Faithful and True sits on a white horse. His robe is sprinkled with blood, and his name is the Word of God. A sword comes from his mouth. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire. The birds are called to feed on the armies.
events.detail: Verse 7 says the Lamb’s wife has made herself ready. Verse 8 describes her clothing: bright, pure, fine linen. Two phrases explain it. “It was given to her” makes the clothing a gift. The linen is also “the righteous acts of the saints.” The verse holds both without choosing. The woman of 17:4 wore purple, scarlet, gold, and pearls.

events.title: Bound deception and final judgment deny death and power their last claim over the dead
events.summary: An angel binds the dragon in the abyss for a thousand years. Those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus live and reign with Christ. This is called the first resurrection. After the thousand years Satan is released and gathers Gog and Magog. Fire devours them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. John sees a great white throne. The dead are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.
events.detail: Verse 11 shows a great white throne, and earth and sky flee from it. Verse 12 shows who stands there: the dead, “the great and the small.” Rank gives no shelter. Two kinds of book are opened. The books record works, and the dead are judged by them. The other is the book of life. Verse 13 adds that the sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead.

events.title: God's dwelling brings renewed life while the holy city reverses the earlier account of luxury
events.summary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea is no more. The holy city, new Jerusalem, comes down from God like a bride. A voice says God’s dwelling is with people. The one on the throne says he is making all things new. An angel shows John the city, with twelve gates named for Israel’s tribes. Its twelve foundations bear the names of the Lamb’s apostles. The city is pure gold, and its gates are pearls. It has no temple or sun, for God and the Lamb light it.
events.detail: Verse 3 announces that God will live with people. Verse 4 says what his presence removes. He wipes every tear, as 7:17 promised. Then four things end: death, mourning, crying, and pain. The verse gives the reason: “The first things have passed away.” The book has shown those first things in its seals, trumpets, and bowls. Verse 5 answers them with one sentence from the throne: all things new.

events.title: The river and tree make life available while the final invitation requires faithful hearing
events.summary: The angel shows John the river of life flowing from the throne. The tree of life grows beside it, and its leaves heal the nations. God’s servants will see his face, and there will be no night. Jesus says he is coming soon. John falls before the angel and is again told to worship God. He is told not to seal the book, for the time is near. A warning forbids adding to or taking from the book’s words. The book ends with a prayer for the Lord Jesus to come.
events.detail: Verse 1 shows the river of the water of life, and verse 2 the tree. Verse 17 turns the vision into an invitation. The Spirit and the bride say “Come.” Each hearer is told to pass the word on. Then the thirsty are invited, and the water is free. In 21:6 the one on the throne made the same offer. Chapter 18 showed a city where everything had a price.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province

regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

guides.title: Revelation: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Different messages test endurance and conduct without making earlier faithfulness sufficient
steps.text: Verses 2–3 praise Ephesus for work, endurance, and testing false apostles. Verse 4 still holds one thing against it: it left its first love. Verse 5 gives three commands in order. Remember where you fell from, repent, and do the first works. Past labor does not replace them. The warning is concrete: the lampstand will be moved from its place. In 1:20 a lampstand is an assembly, so the assembly itself is at risk.

steps.title: The slain Lamb's worthiness changes grief into shared praise and hope of redeemed life
steps.text: Verse 4 shows John weeping because no one can open the book. Verse 5 announces a Lion, and verse 6 shows a slain Lamb. The song in verse 9 says why this Lamb is worthy. The reason is not strength: “for you were killed.” His blood bought people for God. They come from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Verse 10 adds what they become: a kingdom and priests.

steps.title: Worship becomes coercion when deceptive signs and economic exclusion support the beast's power
steps.text: Verses 13–15 show the second beast using signs and the threat of death. Verses 16–17 add a quieter pressure. Everyone, small and great, rich and poor, free and slave, receives a mark. Verse 17 states its use: no one can buy or sell without it. Worship is thus enforced through the market. Verse 10 has already told the saints what this requires: endurance and faith. Verse 18 calls for wisdom about the number.

steps.title: God's dwelling brings renewed life while the holy city reverses the earlier account of luxury
steps.text: Verse 3 announces that God will live with people. Verse 4 says what his presence removes. He wipes every tear, as 7:17 promised. Then four things end: death, mourning, crying, and pain. The verse gives the reason: “The first things have passed away.” The book has shown those first things in its seals, trumpets, and bowls. Verse 5 answers them with one sentence from the throne: all things new.

chapterMaps.narrative: The book calls itself a revelation of Jesus Christ, sent to John. John writes to seven assemblies in Asia. He was on the island of Patmos because of God’s word. On the Lord’s day he hears a voice like a trumpet. He sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands. His eyes are like fire, and a sharp sword comes from his mouth. John falls at his feet like a dead man. The figure tells him to write, and says the lampstands are the seven assemblies.

chapterMaps.note: Markers show the seven addressed cities and the island of Patmos. Heavenly and symbolic settings have no marker.
chapterMaps.narrative: John writes four messages from Christ. Ephesus has worked hard and tested false apostles but has left its first love. Smyrna is poor and yet rich, and will suffer for ten days. Pergamum holds fast where Satan’s throne is, yet some hold the teaching of Balaam. Thyatira has love and service but tolerates a woman called Jezebel. Each message ends with a promise to the one who overcomes. Each tells those with ears to hear what the Spirit says.

chapterMaps.narrative: John writes three more messages. Sardis has a name for being alive and is dead. A few there have not soiled their clothes. Philadelphia has little power, has kept Christ’s word, and has an open door. Laodicea is neither cold nor hot and will be spat out. It says it is rich, yet it is poor, blind, and naked. Christ counsels it to buy gold, white clothes, and eye salve from him. He stands at the door and knocks.

chapterMaps.narrative: John sees a door open in heaven and is called up. One sits on a throne there and shines like jasper and sardius. A rainbow surrounds the throne. Twenty-four elders sit on thrones in white with golden crowns. Seven lamps burn, and a sea like glass lies before the throne. Four living creatures, like a lion, a calf, a man, and an eagle, never rest. They say, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty.” The elders fall down and cast their crowns before the throne.

chapterMaps.narrative: John sees a book in the right hand of the one on the throne. It is sealed with seven seals. An angel asks who is worthy to open it, and no one is found. John weeps. An elder says the Lion of the tribe of Judah has overcome. John looks and sees a Lamb standing as though it had been slain. The Lamb takes the book, and the creatures and elders sing a new song. Countless angels and every creature join the praise.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Lamb opens six seals. A rider on a white horse goes out to conquer. A red horse takes peace from the earth, and a black horse brings scarce food. A pale horse carries Death, and Hades follows. At the fifth seal John sees under the altar those killed for God’s word. They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. At the sixth seal the earth quakes and the sky rolls up. Kings and slaves hide and ask who is able to stand.

chapterMaps.narrative: Four angels hold back the winds until God’s servants are sealed. John hears the number: 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel. Then he sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation. They wear white robes and hold palm branches. They cry that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. An elder says they have come out of the great suffering. They washed their robes white in the Lamb’s blood. They will never hunger or thirst again.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Lamb opens the seventh seal, and heaven is silent for half an hour. Seven angels receive seven trumpets. Another angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints at the golden altar. He fills the censer with fire and throws it to the earth. The first trumpet burns a third of the earth and trees. The second and third strike a third of the sea and the rivers. The fourth darkens a third of the sun, moon, and stars. An eagle cries woe for the three trumpets still to come.

chapterMaps.narrative: At the fifth trumpet a star falls and opens the pit of the abyss. Smoke rises, and locusts come out with power like scorpions. They may not kill, but they torment people without God’s seal for five months. Their king is called Abaddon, or Apollyon. At the sixth trumpet four angels bound at the Euphrates are released. An army of horsemen kills a third of mankind with fire and sulfur. The survivors do not repent of idols. They do not repent of murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts.

chapterMaps.narrative: A mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow on his head. He holds a little open book and stands on sea and land. Seven thunders speak, and John is told not to write their words. The angel swears that there will be no more delay. A voice tells John to take the book from the angel. The angel says it will taste sweet and turn the stomach bitter. John eats it, and it is so. He is told he must prophesy again about many peoples and kings.

chapterMaps.narrative: John is given a reed to measure God’s temple. Two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth for 1,260 days. Fire comes from their mouths, and they can shut the sky. The beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie in the street. People celebrate for three and a half days. Then the breath of life enters them, and they go up to heaven. An earthquake follows. The seventh trumpet sounds, and voices say the world’s kingdom has become the Lord’s.

chapterMaps.narrative: A woman clothed with the sun cries out in labor. A great red dragon with seven heads waits to devour her child. Her son, who will rule the nations, is caught up to God. The woman flees to the wilderness. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him down to the earth. A voice calls him the accuser and says the brothers overcame him. The dragon pursues the woman, and the earth helps her. He goes to make war on the rest of her offspring.

chapterMaps.narrative: A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and seven heads. The dragon gives it power, and one head has a healed death wound. The whole earth marvels and worships it. It speaks blasphemies and makes war on the saints for forty-two months. A second beast rises from the earth with two horns like a lamb. It works signs and makes people worship the first beast’s image. It puts a mark on the right hand or forehead of all. The number of the beast is 666.

chapterMaps.narrative: John sees the Lamb on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name. They sing a new song and follow the Lamb wherever he goes. An angel flies with eternal good news for every nation. A second says Babylon has fallen. A third warns that those who worship the beast will drink God’s wrath. A voice blesses the dead who die in the Lord. One like a son of man reaps the earth’s harvest. An angel gathers the grapes and throws them into the winepress of God’s wrath.

chapterMaps.narrative: John sees seven angels with the seven last plagues. Those who overcame the beast stand on a sea of glass mixed with fire. They hold harps of God. They sing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb. The song says all nations will come and worship. The temple of the tabernacle of the testimony opens in heaven. One of the living creatures gives the angels seven golden bowls of wrath. Smoke fills the temple, and no one can enter until the plagues end.

chapterMaps.narrative: A voice tells the seven angels to pour out the bowls. Sores, a sea of blood, and rivers of blood follow. The sun scorches people, and they blaspheme and do not repent. The beast’s kingdom is darkened. The Euphrates dries up for the kings from the east. Three unclean spirits like frogs gather the kings for war. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying, “It is done,” and a great earthquake. Great hail falls, and people blaspheme God.

chapterMaps.narrative: An angel shows John a woman seated on a scarlet beast. She wears purple and gold and is drunk with the saints’ blood. Her name is “Babylon the Great.” The angel explains the mystery. The beast’s seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings. The ten horns are ten kings who give their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and he will overcome them. The horns will hate the woman, the great city, and burn her.

chapterMaps.narrative: An angel cries that Babylon the great has fallen. Another voice calls God’s people to come out of her. Her sins have reached heaven, and she will be repaid double. Kings who shared her luxury weep at the smoke of her burning. Merchants weep because no one buys their cargo. The list runs from gold and spices to the bodies and souls of people. Shipmasters cry out that such wealth was ruined in one hour. A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, and the city’s music stops.

chapterMaps.narrative: A great crowd in heaven praises God for judging the great prostitute. A voice announces the Lamb’s marriage, and his wife has made herself ready. John falls to worship the angel and is told to worship God. Heaven opens, and a rider called Faithful and True sits on a white horse. His robe is sprinkled with blood, and his name is the Word of God. A sword comes from his mouth. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire. The birds are called to feed on the armies.

chapterMaps.narrative: An angel binds the dragon in the abyss for a thousand years. Those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus live and reign with Christ. This is called the first resurrection. After the thousand years Satan is released and gathers Gog and Magog. Fire devours them, and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. John sees a great white throne. The dead are judged by what is written in the books. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.

The one on the throne says he is making all things new. An angel shows John the city, with twelve gates named for Israel’s tribes. Its twelve foundations bear the names of the Lamb’s apostles. The city is pure gold, and its gates are pearls. It has no temple or sun, for God and the Lamb light it.

chapterMaps.narrative: The angel shows John the river of life flowing from the throne. The tree of life grows beside it, and its leaves heal the nations. God’s servants will see his face, and there will be no night. Jesus says he is coming soon. John falls before the angel and is again told to worship God. He is told not to seal the book, for the time is near. A warning forbids adding to or taking from the book’s words. The book ends with a prayer for the Lord Jesus to come.
